title: New Zealand’s banks could keep lending in a severe downturn, but dividends and funding would come under pressure
summary: New Zealand’s financial system remained able to support the economy, in the Reserve Bank’s assessment on 17 November, even as the risk of a significant external shock rose. Local financial stress had generally eased from its peak in 2025. That left households and financial institutions in a better starting position, but it offered limited protection against several shocks arriving together. An energy disruption could lift import costs and bond yields just as a correction in richly valued AI-related assets tightened offshore funding. Weaker demand from trading partners could reduce export receipts at the same time. Relatively favourable funding conditions and resilient foreign growth had so far contained these channels (chapter 1).

A joint stress test with the Australian supervisor illustrates the difference between the ability to keep operating and the capacity to distribute profits. The scenario combined a prolonged oil shock with deep Australian and New Zealand recessions and substantial property losses. Among the four large New Zealand banks, aggregate common equity tier 1 capital fell from 13.2% of risk-weighted assets to a trough of 8.5%. Banks remained above regulatory minima and were generally able to keep lending. They nevertheless entered their capital buffers, triggering restrictions on dividends and requirements for capital restoration. Loan losses reduced capital, while deteriorating credit quality raised risk-weighted assets. The latter contributed more to New Zealand banks’ capital-ratio decline than in Australia, partly because of different regulatory treatments. Parent-bank support could also be harder to obtain precisely when both countries were under stress (p. 14).

The domestic evidence was mixed. Early mortgage arrears had declined. Based on mortgage rates and market pricing at publication, however, the Reserve Bank expected the average rate borrowers actually paid to rise from about 4.8% to 5.4% over the following year. Households that bought near the 2021 market peak with small deposits in Auckland or Wellington could find it difficult to refinance even while meeting repayments. In commercial property development and parts of construction, cash flows remained under pressure. Farmers entered the period with stronger incomes and balance sheets, although a weak harvest or an increase in costs would still hurt. The report retained existing loan-to-value settings following its July review (pp. 10–13).

Funding and margins affect how banks absorb those pressures. Deposits provided 64% of funding. Customers had moved towards on-call accounts when the reward for locking up money narrowed, then back towards term deposits when banks raised rates. Such switching can raise funding costs before a bank experiences any loss of deposits. Digital channels and open banking may also make moving balances faster. Outcomes depend on customer behaviour, how deposits are distributed and the availability of credible protection. The updated liquidity assumptions distinguish insured balances from large corporate deposits. Historical banking-system stability cannot by itself establish that one institution’s deposits would remain stable during a confidence shock (chapter 3, figures 3.5–3.6 and box B).

Net interest margins have generally been between 2% and 2.5% since the mid-2000s. Greater mortgage competition, the weight of relatively low-margin housing lending and competition for deposits all affect the outlook. Banks’ hedges smooth part of the interest-rate effect over time. Higher market rates consequently have no single immediate implication for earnings. The report treats earnings as a source of future capital and distinguishes softer profitability from the banks’ strong existing capital and liquidity positions (chapter 3 and chapter 4).

The conclusions differ across insurers. In a reverse stress test, the five largest life insurers and three largest health insurers generally needed combinations of severe shocks to breach solvency requirements. Pandemic-related mortality or morbidity alongside impaired reinsurance mattered for life insurers. Medical costs, higher use of health services and limited scope to raise premiums mattered for health insurers. The exercise identifies combinations capable of producing failure, without estimating their probability. Cyber and operational disruptions could compound losses across both insurance and banking, a reason the Reserve Bank stressed continuity of critical services alongside financial buffers (table 1.1 and chapter 4).

questions.question: How would income, capital and distributions change for individual banks under a joint funding and credit shock?
questions.detail: The four-bank aggregate preserves regulatory minima yet breaches buffers in the test. Compare each bank’s starting capital, dividend policy, wholesale maturity ladder and credit concentrations using its prudential and financial disclosures. Stress its access to Australian parent funding alongside domestic losses. The same system-wide capital result could imply quite different outcomes for bank equity, subordinated debt and senior funding.

questions.question: How sensitive are margins and liquidity to the movement of existing deposits?
questions.detail: The report shows substantial switching between on-call and term accounts as interest-rate incentives change. Estimate the repricing of existing balances separately from outright deposit losses, using the chart data, deposit rates and banks’ maturity disclosures. Identify uninsured corporate concentration and the extent to which interest-rate hedges delay earnings effects. This would help judge whether competitive repricing or an actual funding shortfall is the more immediate risk.

questions.question: Which borrowers would encounter cash-flow stress before it appeared in aggregate arrears?
questions.detail: The expected rise in average mortgage rates combines borrowers on different refixing schedules, with different equity and incomes. Compare loan vintages and regional house prices with refixing dates, hardship applications and early arrears, while tracking job losses. For business credit, examine construction and rural portfolios separately. A change concentrated among highly leveraged recent borrowers would have different loss implications from a small broad rise in arrears.
